values: BraTS research papers and learning notes
Ten studies from the existing reading collection, 2023–2026. Filter Paper ID to read one paper. Source-reported findings are not independently reproduced here.
Prepared 20 October 2026. This is a focused collection, not an exhaustive literature search.
“Research opportunity” and “NeuroScan lesson” are our analysis. A limitation may instead be a boundary of the available evidence; these are labeled explicitly.

LiteFreqMamba: lightweight frequency-enhanced Mamba for efficient 3D brain tumor segmentation
Frontiers in Oncology
Segment a 3D tumor accurately with a smaller model, while retaining the thin and irregular edges that efficient models can overlook.
The paper targets two competing needs: seeing the overall tumor shape and preserving small boundary details without excessive memory use.

LiteFreqMamba separates broad image structure from fine changes, combines Mamba with attention, and filters information passed to the decoder. In simple terms, it studies both the big outline and the small edges.
BraTS 2020 and BraTS 2021. Section 4.1 describes local patient-wise evaluation; these results are not automatically official hidden-test leaderboard scores.
The authors report competitive segmentation with 4.96 million parameters. This supports an efficiency claim under their protocol, not a guarantee of fast CPU deployment.
The authors assume all MRI sequences are available. They also acknowledge that better segmentation alone does not directly prove their explanation about frequency bias.
Our analysis: test whether this design remains useful when a sequence is absent and whether its memory and speed advantages survive on the actual deployment hardware.
Start with a measured baseline. Compare full-volume Dice, boundary error, memory and total processing time on the same patients before replacing our U-Net.
Full primary article. Local benchmark evaluation, not an independently reproduced result.

PF-CMNet: Progressive Frequency-Aware Cross-Modal Network with Missing-Modality Distillation for 3D Brain Tumor Segmentation
Brain Sciences
Improve tumor boundaries and keep segmentation useful when one or more MRI sequences are missing.
Weak image contrast, very small enhancing regions and uncertain tissue borders make prediction difficult. Losing a sequence removes further evidence.
PF-CMNet combines frequency-aware MRI fusion, gradual boundary reconstruction and teacher-student learning. A teacher sees complete scans; a student learns with some inputs removed.
BraTS 2021 and MSD Task01 BrainTumour. The missing-input experiments remove entire sequences rather than simulating every possible image artifact.
The paper reports average Dice of 88.2% on BraTS 2021. In its specified missing-T1ce test, average Dice is 58.39%; that is an average, not an ET-only score.
The authors identify remaining weak-ET and boundary failures, and call for further multicenter and workflow-level validation.
Our analysis: a missing channel, a motion-damaged channel and a misaligned channel are different problems. Test each separately, and measure the entire application rather than just model execution.
Use a clearly labeled missing-input test table. Keep failure examples beside the scores, especially for small enhancing regions, instead of showing only successful masks.
Primary article and existing detailed reading notes. Missing-sequence results are simulated channel removal.

A lightweight brain tumor segmentation network based on cross-modality feature fusion
Engineering Applications of Artificial Intelligence
Combine information from four MRI sequences while keeping the segmentation network compact.
Each sequence highlights different image features. Mixing them poorly can hide useful information, while larger fusion networks increase computation.
Four encoder branches learn from the sequences separately. Modality-specific attention and cross-modal fusion then combine the useful features. Think of four observers comparing their notes.
BraTS 2021: 1251 patients with a local 8:1:1 train/validation/test split, according to the publisher dataset section.
The abstract reports WT Dice 93.12%, TC 89.50%, ET 85.92%, with 3.66 million parameters. These are the authors’ local-protocol results, not a fair ranking against other papers.
The verified material establishes benchmark testing. It does not by itself establish reliable hospital deployment or support for every incomplete-input combination.
Our analysis: does the extra branching improve segmentation enough to justify its actual processing cost? Missing-input robustness must be measured, not inferred from a four-branch design.
Compare our early-fusion U-Net with a small multi-branch variant. Use identical patient splits and training budgets, then measure both accuracy and real inference time.
Publisher abstract, method and dataset excerpts. Not a full independent protocol audit.

Collaborative encoding attributed hybrid attention knowledge distillation for missing-modality brain tumor segmentation
Biomedical Signal Processing and Control
Segment brain tumors when some MRI sequences are unavailable, without first generating replacement images.
A model trained only with complete inputs can lose important information at deployment. The remaining sequences still need to exchange complementary features.
The student combines modality-specific vision Transformers with a Mamba encoder. Attention-based distillation transfers information from a complete-input teacher to the student.
The publisher abstract explicitly names BraTS 2020 and BraTS 2021. The journal issue is March 2026, although the DOI contains 2025.
The abstract reports improvements over missing-modality comparison methods, including mmFormer and M2FTrans. No unsupported numerical score is supplied here.
This profile is based on accessible publisher abstract and introduction material. Detailed failure rates and author-stated limitations are not established by that evidence alone.

Our analysis: the teacher and dual encoders add training work. It remains a useful project question whether distillation beats simpler sequence dropout under the same student-model and training budget.
First train a sequence-dropout baseline. Then add distillation and test all 15 nonempty combinations of four inputs, recording training cost as well as segmentation quality.
Publisher abstract, highlights, introduction and dataset excerpts. Detailed author limitations were not independently established.

Medical SAM adapter: Adapting segment anything model for medical image segmentation
Medical Image Analysis
Adapt the general Segment Anything Model to medical segmentation, including three-dimensional scans, without retraining every parameter.
Medical boundaries and 3D anatomy differ from the natural images used to train the original model. Useful prompts also need to influence the segmentation.
Medical SAM Adapter adds trainable adapter modules, Space-Depth Transpose and Hyper-Prompting. An adapter is a small trainable addition to a larger pretrained model.
BraTS 2021 appears in Section 4.1 among several medical datasets. The article states 1280 scans; clarify that count and the release before reproducing the study.
The work demonstrates parameter-efficient adaptation across medical benchmarks. Fewer trainable parameters do not necessarily mean that the complete inference model is small.
The system is prompt-conditioned. Its results should not be treated as a direct comparison with fully automatic segmentation unless the prompting conditions are matched.
Our analysis: how much human effort does a usable correction require? Prompts derived from a reference mask could make a comparison unrealistically easy. Evaluate prompts available to a real user.
For interactive correction, record the original mask, each edit, correction time and remaining error. Compare automatic output with a fixed amount of human assistance.
Primary journal article and earlier dataset-section reading notes. Resolve the reported cohort-count discrepancy before replication.

A 3D lightweight network with Roberts edge enhancement model (LR-Net) for brain tumor segmentation
Scientific Reports
Reduce model size and computation while preserving useful information about the whole tumor and its fuzzy edges.
Local convolutions can miss broader context. Combining them with large Transformers can be expensive, especially for 3D volumes.
LR-Net uses spatial shifts, pixel-shuffle upsampling, channel attention and Roberts edge enhancement. These operations move and combine features while emphasizing intensity changes near boundaries.
The abstract and experiments explicitly include BraTS 2019, BraTS 2020 and BraTS 2021.
The authors report 4.72 million parameters and a Dice value of 0.860 on BraTS 2021. Check the region averaging and split before comparing this figure with another model.
The reported overlap is not perfect. The abstract does not establish clinical reliability or performance on our CPU; these are evidence limits rather than claimed author admissions.
Our analysis: an intensity edge can be noise or normal tissue, not just a tumor border. Test whether edge enhancement remains helpful under controlled noise, low contrast and scanner changes.
Compare a baseline with and without the edge component. Keep the data split fixed and report small-lesion misses, boundary errors and measured runtime.
Full primary article. Reported benchmark results have not been reproduced in NeuroScan.

Deep learning-driven modality imputation and subregion segmentation to enhance high-grade glioma grading
BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making
Estimate missing MRI sequences and segment tumor subregions to support investigation of high-grade glioma grading.
Missing images limit the available information, while complex tumor regions are difficult to outline and interpret consistently.
A PatchGAN-based generator with Transformer-related blocks estimates missing views. A U-Net variant then segments subregions. The generated view is an estimate, not a newly acquired scan.
Methods identify 1251 BraTS 2021 cases and an external clinical cohort of 181 cases.
The study reports benefits from combining imputation and segmentation. It also finds that less experienced radiologists did not show a statistically significant AUC improvement.
The authors identify limited multicenter and scanner diversity, plus a small heterogeneous clinical cohort. One external center cannot represent every clinical setting.

Our analysis: visual realism is insufficient. A generated scan must preserve the lesion information needed by segmentation. Measure whether generated inputs change or erase small regions, and keep synthetic images clearly labeled.
Compare real complete inputs, incomplete inputs and generated replacements on the same patients. Do not add grading claims to our segmentation app without a separate validated grading task.
Full primary article. Includes an external clinical cohort; do not describe it as benchmark-only.

Brain tumor segmentation using deep learning: high performance with minimized MRI data
Frontiers in Radiology
Find whether fewer MRI sequences can still provide useful tumor segmentation.
Four-sequence inputs create acquisition and data requirements. A smaller input set is useful only if it retains the information needed for the target regions.
The authors compare 3D U-Net models using T1C only, FLAIR only, T1C plus FLAIR, and all four sequences.
Training uses 285 BraTS 2018 cases. The 358-case test set includes 292 BraTS 2021 cases and 66 BraTS 2018 cases. BraTS 2021 is used for testing here.
On the combined test set, T1C plus FLAIR gives ET Dice 0.867 and TC Dice 0.926. These are not BraTS 2021-only results.
The authors note that the four-input model may not have converged within 60 epochs. Tumor locations and the mixture of tumor grades also limit generalization.

Our analysis: equal epochs do not guarantee equally trained models. Test convergence before concluding that two sequences are inherently better than four. Selected fixed combinations are not equivalent to arbitrary missing-input support.
Compare two-input and four-input baselines using documented stopping rules, best validation checkpoints and the same held-out patients. This experiment should not guide clinical scan omission.
Full primary article. Mixed-year test results must not be relabeled as BraTS 2021-only results.

Lightweight MRI Brain Tumor Segmentation Enhanced by Hierarchical Feature Fusion
Tomography
Preserve small tumor details while keeping a segmentation model relatively lightweight.
Summarizing a volume can remove fine structures, and restoring image resolution does not automatically restore information already lost.
EHFF combines adaptive feature learning, hierarchical weighting and feature retention. It gives the decoder both broad context and more detailed information from earlier stages.
BraTS 2021 is explicitly used. The paper reports five-fold cross-validation; Section 3.4 describes component ablations on fold 4.
The abstract reports Dice of 88.57% for ET, 91.53% for TC and 93.09% for WT. These region-specific results are not generic voxel accuracy.
Section 3.5 acknowledges that large-kernel processing can still lose fine details despite the micro-focus module.

Our analysis: repeat the component-removal experiments across more seeds or folds to determine whether each module helps consistently. Also examine very small lesions; a strong overall average can conceal their errors.
Test weighting alone, detail retention alone, both together and the unchanged baseline. Save per-patient masks so numerical gains can be linked to visible changes.
Primary article and earlier section-level reading notes. Main cross-validation and component ablations use different coverage.

Brain Tumor Segmentation for Multi-Modal MRI with Missing Information
Journal of Digital Imaging
Make one segmentation network more tolerant of missing MRI sequences using a simple training change.
Complete-input training leaves a model unprepared when one or more sequences disappear. The missing contrast-enhanced sequence is particularly important for enhancing tumor.
Sequence dropout randomly removes input sequences during training. The model practices with incomplete information instead of encountering that situation only after deployment.
The paper explicitly uses BraTS 2021 and additionally evaluates 30 TCGA cases. It should not be described as having no external evaluation.
With T1, T2 and FLAIR but no T1ce, ET Dice improves from 0.143 to 0.486. This is a large improvement, but substantial segmentation error remains.
The results show that missing T1ce remains difficult. External evaluation is limited in size, and complete sequence removal does not represent all possible scan artifacts.
Our analysis: evaluate noisy and misaligned inputs separately from absent inputs. Check patient identity and cohort overlap before calling any external comparison fully independent.
This is a sensible first robustness experiment for our U-Net. Train a new checkpoint, preserve some complete-input examples and evaluate all 15 nonempty input subsets before allowing partial uploads.
Primary article and earlier section-level reading notes. Small external cohort is present; independence still requires patient-level checks.

values: Recommended order: establish trustworthy full-volume results, then test missing-input robustness, then optimize the architecture. All experiments below are proposed, not completed.

A reproducible application is useful engineering. A research contribution needs a justified question, fair comparisons and evidence of what changed. Combining existing ideas is not automatically novel.
Amber cells are editable status fields.

Save patient split IDs, data release, code revision, seed, preprocessing config and checkpoint hash. Record validation only when measured. Select the best checkpoint by a predefined validation metric. Block synthetic output in research runs.
Re-evaluate the exact deployed postprocessing on a locked patient-level test set. Inspect predictions and metadata. Do not compare historical training curves with new test scores.
WT/TC/ET Dice and HD95 (mm), case count, failures, provenance completeness.
Replace center-crop-only inference with overlapping 3D windows and probability blending. Verify shape, orientation and affine consistency. Add tests for lesions near volume edges.
Compare crop-only and tiled inference using the same checkpoint to isolate coverage. Then separately test tumor-aware patch training. Keep geometry and postprocessing fixed.
Full-volume regional Dice, HD95, sensitivity, tumor outside crop, peak RAM and seconds/case.
Add sequence dropout during training and retain complete-input examples. Record a modality-presence mask. Retrain a new model before permitting partial uploads.
Baseline versus dropout, same split and architecture. Evaluate all 15 nonempty subsets of T1/T1ce/T2/FLAIR. Treat absent inputs, noise and misalignment as separate tests.
Primary candidate: ET Dice without T1ce. Also TC/WT and complete-input performance with paired uncertainty intervals.
Profile load, normalization, neural prediction, saving and response separately. Test a smaller U-Net before complex Mamba/fusion modules. Keep model weights loaded in a worker.
Use identical full volumes, hardware and precision. Report cold and warm timing and repeated runs. Compare resource use only at matched quality constraints.
Median/p95 end-to-end seconds, model-only seconds, RAM/VRAM, model size and regional Dice.
Add one detail-preserving feature or boundary-aware loss at a time. Keep a balanced mixture of tumor and background training patches.
Baseline, new component alone, sampling change alone, both. Use identical splits and repeated seeds. Include noise/low-contrast stress tests.
Dice, HD95, lesion-wise recall, false positives and performance by predeclared lesion-size bands.
Train a dedicated T1ce+FLAIR model and a four-input model. Save comparable convergence curves and best validation checkpoints.
Use matched tuning budgets and documented stopping rules; equal epochs alone can be unfair. This is distinct from arbitrary missing-input inference.
Per-region full-volume metrics, runtime, resource use and failure examples on the same patients.
Add editable masks only after automatic output is reliable. Preserve original mask, revisions, prompt locations and edit time.
Compare automatic predictions with a fixed time or number of realistic prompts. Do not use ground-truth boxes as if they were free user input.
Remaining error, correction time, inter-user variation and revision traceability.
Treat generated MRI as synthetic and label it. Do not replace acquired scans or add grading claims without task-specific evidence.
Compare complete acquired inputs, incomplete inputs and imputed replacements on the same cases. Prioritize the simpler dropout baseline first.
Downstream segmentation, small-region preservation, failures and runtime, not image realism alone.
Suggested first research question: Does sequence dropout improve missing-T1ce ET segmentation after full-volume coverage is fixed, while retaining acceptable complete-input performance?
Possible contribution: a reproducible quality–robustness–CPU-cost evaluation for a web workflow. Novelty is a hypothesis: extend the literature search before claiming that this has not been done.

values: What the project evidence currently supports
Code inspected on 20 October 2026. The numerical observations below were recorded in the 8 October audit; no new model experiment was run for this workbook.
Two cases with unknown training membership cannot establish generalization, clinical reliability or superiority over a paper.
The prior audit loaded a PyTorch checkpoint and observed a neural forward call for each of two cases. Saved predictions matched those neural outputs.
Supports real model execution for the audited cases, not a claim that every saved or future result is model-generated.
Store inference mode, checkpoint hash and preprocessing version with every output.
Local audit, 8 Oct 2026: status, cases and saved_case_comparisons.
Current inference code generates a synthetic label map when no model is available and returns demo_mode.
A synthetic/demo mask is not a measured medical-model prediction and must not enter an evaluation dataset.
Fail clearly in research mode; keep demonstration outputs labeled and separate.
Code: backend/app/services/inference.py, model selection and demo branch.
Current preprocessing crops larger scans centrally and restores the output into a zero-filled original volume.
Outside-crop anatomy is not predicted. Cropped Dice may greatly exceed full-volume Dice.
Use full-volume tiled inference and test edge lesions and affine alignment.
The current script sets val_loss to train_loss before optional validation, saves the final checkpoint, and configures 40 epochs.
Skipped validation is not independent validation. A script configuration does not prove the actual training history of a particular checkpoint.
Save explicit missing validation values, best-validation checkpoint, split manifest and run metadata.
Code: training/train_brats.py, main training loop and checkpoint export.
The prior audit found stored NCR/ED/ET mean Dice 0.8708 and records of 40 epochs.
These class scores are not WT/TC/ET full-volume held-out performance. The original 20-epoch objective is not supported by these records.
Trace the weights to a specific run and compute common region metrics on a locked independent test set.
There is a functioning research prototype with real neural inference demonstrated on two audited examples.
No complete independent validation study or new-paper superiority claim is established by this workbook.
Complete the baseline protocol, then run one controlled research experiment.
Synthesis of inspected code and the dated local audit, not a new benchmark.
Source: saved offline audit of the production inference function on 8 October 2026. Two cases only. Training split membership unknown; not an independent test cohort.
The web UI and HTTP service were not tested in that audit. These scores are descriptive observations and must not be used to claim “90% proven accuracy.”

values: A defensible study and paper checklist
This is a proposed workflow, not completed research. Amber cells are for your progress and evidence references. “Documented” does not imply clinical approval.
Evidence supports a narrowly stated conclusion under tested conditions; it does not prove universal safety or guarantee publication. Discuss the protocol with Ms. Saira Ishtiaq before training.
Choose one question and one primary endpoint before running the study. Search recent work beyond these ten papers.
Dated protocol, search terms/dates, relevant baselines and a clear statement of what is different.
An attractive interface or copied architecture is not sufficient scientific novelty.
Record BraTS release, subject IDs, counts, permissions and exclusions. Check cross-year and external-cohort overlap.
Dataset manifest with hashes and patient-level duplicates/exclusions log.
A different dataset year does not automatically mean different patients.
Keep every slice, patch and sequence of one person in the same split. Lock test IDs before tuning.
Train/validation/test manifests and an explicit zero-overlap check.
Slice-level splitting can leak patient information into testing.
Verify image-mask orientation, affine, voxel spacing and label mapping. Document annotation provenance and uncertainty.
Geometry tests and visual examples of correct alignment and rejected inputs.
A spatial mismatch can invalidate apparently precise metrics.
Record only measured validation values. Choose checkpoints using validation, never the test set.
Raw run logs, checkpoint selection rule, seed, optimizer and stopping rule.
A training loss copied into validation is not evidence of generalization.
Use a well-defined U-Net baseline. Consider nnU-Net if feasible; document any reimplementation differences.
Same patient split, preprocessing, augmentation and comparable tuning budgets.
Changing many settings at once makes attribution unclear.
Evaluate the saved final labels over the entire volume using deployed postprocessing. Define empty-region behavior beforehand.
Per-patient WT/TC/ET metrics and masks, plus evaluator version and unit tests.
Cropped metrics and overlapping threshold channels are not equivalent to final-label metrics.
For the missing-input study, consider ET Dice without T1ce as primary. Define acceptable complete-input loss before seeing test results.
Predeclared primary outcome, secondary outcomes and justified tolerance.
Choose tolerances with the supervisor; no universal safe Dice cutoff is assumed.
Use patient-level paired comparisons with confidence intervals. For repeated scans, resample at patient level. Predefine tests and multiplicity handling.
Effect size and paired bootstrap interval, analysis code, seed and sampling plan.
A tiny p-value does not establish clinical usefulness; an inconclusive result is not equivalence.
Budget repeated seeds or folds, and justify the test sample size using planned precision or power. Do not treat voxels as independent patients.
Compute budget, sample-size rationale and variability across runs.
Three seeds may expose instability but are not a universal adequacy rule.
Change one component at a time and repeat key comparisons. Keep test data out of model selection.
Baseline, component A, component B and combined experiment results where relevant.
An improvement needs attribution, not just a final model score.
Test all 15 nonempty modality subsets for a missing-input model. Test noise and misalignment separately. Evaluate a genuinely independent cohort if available.
Results by region and subset, failed cases and independently verified cohort provenance.
Simulated missing channels are narrower evidence than hospital deployment.
Measure cold/warm and total workflow time on named hardware. Report loading, preprocessing, prediction and export separately.
Repeated timings, median/p95 latency, RAM/VRAM, precision and software versions.
Parameter count and FLOPs are not measured web-application latency.
Inspect worst and typical cases, small lesions and relevant subgroups. Report failure counts and missing outputs.
Predeclared size bands, error gallery and subgroup denominators.
A high average can hide systematic misses or false positives.
Save code version, environment, seeds, weights/checksums, splits and scripts. Respect dataset sharing and privacy restrictions.
Reproduction instructions, accessible code/configs, data availability statement and limitations.
Do not publish patient data or claim reproducibility from screenshots alone.
Write methods and limitations honestly. Use the CLAIM checklist as a reporting aid. Agree actual author contributions with the team.
Completed manuscript checklist, citation verification and supervisor review.
A reporting checklist improves transparency but is not experimental or clinical validation.
Segmentation assigns a region to each voxel. Classification assigns a category to a case or region.
A segmentation experiment does not validate tumor grade or molecular-marker prediction.
Different MRI contrasts. T1ce, T1C and T1Gd refer to contrast-enhanced T1 in these studies.
Missing T1ce removes an acquired source of enhancement information.
ET = label 4. TC = labels 1 + 4. WT = labels 1 + 2 + 4 in the BraTS 2021 convention.
Verify remapping if software internally uses consecutive class IDs. Label 2 includes peritumoral edematous/invaded tissue.
Overlap between prediction and reference: twice the intersection divided by the sum of their sizes. Higher is better.
Define the both-empty case before testing. Dice is not general voxel accuracy.
A high-percentile boundary-distance measure. Lower is better when regions are present.
Use physical spacing. Predefine treatment of empty predictions or empty references.
Background occupies many more voxels than a small tumor region.
High overall accuracy can coexist with missing the tumor. Use region and lesion-level metrics.
Some tissue transitions are gradual, so even reference outlines may be uncertain.
A sharper displayed edge is not automatically a more correct boundary.
Remove entire MRI channels during training so the model practices with missing inputs.
Requires training and testing; merely allowing missing uploads does not make an old model robust.
Distillation teaches a student from a teacher. Imputation generates an estimate of a missing image.
Transferred knowledge and generated images do not restore an actually acquired scan.
An ablation isolates one design choice. An external test evaluates a separate data source.
Verify patient independence; novelty or clinical validity does not follow automatically.
An interval expressing uncertainty about an estimated effect under the analysis assumptions.
Report patient-level differences and intervals, not just one winning mean.
Parameters count learned weights. FLOPs estimate arithmetic. Latency is elapsed time.
Different measures answer different questions; compare hardware and full pipelines.
Turn the experiments into a paper
Define the practical problem, summarize the closest prior work and state one testable contribution.
Avoid “first” or “state of the art” without a sufficiently broad search and fair evidence.
Describe data, splits, preprocessing, model, baseline, training, metrics and statistical analysis.
Give enough detail to repeat the exact experiment. State planned versus exploratory analyses.
Report complete and missing-input results, paired differences, uncertainty, ablations and resource use.
Use measured results only. Include unfavorable and failed cases, not fabricated target values.
Show cohort/split flow, architecture or pipeline, per-region results, paired differences and failure examples.
Do not draw a leaderboard from incompatible published scores. Use the same held-out patients for model comparisons.
Explain what improved, what did not, plausible reasons and how the result relates to the ten papers.
Separate evidence from interpretation and identify what additional study would change the conclusion.
State dataset scope, sample size, uncertainty, external-testing limits and reproducibility resources.
Benchmark validation is not prospective clinical validation. Declare data and code access restrictions.
Hamza Mustafa and Wajid Ali contributed to the project. Supervisor: Ms. Saira Ishtiaq.
Agree author order and specific contributions with everyone before submission; supervision alone does not determine authorship.
Dataset tasks, region definitions, preparation and evaluation context.
Medical-imaging AI reporting checklist; a reporting aid, not proof of model validity.
